summary: Weekly POC sync focused on unit economics (tokens/sec/$), observed caching benefits, and batching tradeoffs. Redwood SE reported baseline throughput and cost projections; customer asked for more representative prompts and an extended benchmark. Agreement to run a 5k-token stress run with cache on/off and fixed batching, and to schedule a security/VPC follow-up. Consensus: caching gives strong savings for repeat prefixes; batching improves tokens/sec but increases tail latency — need to balance for Auriga's interactive use cases.
topics: KV/prefix caching benefits and hit rates
Batching size vs tail latency tradeoffs
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-08-12
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Ethan (Redwood SE), Lina (CSM), Priya (Auriga - Lead ML), Daniel (Platform), Sonia (Product), Ravi (SRE)
---
[00:00] Maya: ok uh good afternoon everyone, thanks for joining. quick agenda: recap last week's numbers, ethan will share the baseline throughput numbers, then discuss caching and batching tradeoffs, and lock next steps. sound good?
[00:18] Priya: yep that works for us. we want to focus on the tokens per dollar metric — specifically what to expect in user facing flows where we have ~200–800 token responses usually but some long context cases.
[00:32] Ethan: cool. so quick recap — we ran the initial pilot on redwood-hosted gw, baseline model variant it was the 13B quantized run, continuous batching enabled, KV cache disabled for that first pass. the baseline numbers: about 18k tokens/sec per GPU, which maps to roughly 0.018 tokens/sec per dollar on the hosted price in our sheet — uh sorry, let me rephrase — 18k tokens/sec for the whole pool, which we normalized to tokens/sec per $ using the pilot pool hourly cost.
[01:05] Daniel: real quick — can you remind us which kernel optimizations were turned on? last call there was mention of attention fusion and a custom matmul path.
[01:12] Ethan: yes, attention fusion on, matmul auto-tuned for A100s. also we used the quantization profile q4_0 — that gave good perf but slightly noisier outputs. transcription note: sometimes folks see the q profile referenced as Q four o.
[01:28] Priya: noise in outputs is a concern. for our ranking scoring we saw a 2% shift in top-1 on the regen tests last week. is that from quant or batch effects?
[01:37] Ethan: likely a mix. quantization contributes, especially on low-frequency tokens; batching can change tokenization alignments and generation timing, so sometimes the beam/best-of differences appear. we'll run an eval on your prompt set to isolate.
[01:49] Sonia: also curious about caching — for our app many users hit similar prefixes, e.g., when they ask about account summaries. what's realistic cache hit rate here?
[01:58] Ethan: based on the sample traffic you gave earlier, we estimate prefix reuse maybe 18–25% in the user query paths. with prefix canonicalization that could be higher — maybe 30–35%. those hit rates translate to 40–60% token savings in some scenarios because a cached KV avoids compute for prefix tokens. caveat: if users provide unique long contexts, hit rate drops.
[02:24] Priya: the cache sounds promising. can you quantify cost delta if we enable KV cache — tokens/sec/$ up how much?
[02:32] Ethan: yes. with cache enabled and a 30% hit rate the effective tokens/sec per dollar improves about 1.6x in our model. if we get to 45% hit it could be ~2x. again depends on model variant and seq lengths. these numbers assume no additional replication cost for the cache; in dedicated we might mirror caches which adds some infra cost.
[02:55] Ravi: question on private deployment: what's the impact on network egress and KMS calls if we do remote KMS for wrap/unwrap? we have strict egress budgets.
[03:04] Maya: good call — we'll need to map out KMS call volumes. short answer: KMS calls are infrequent (key unwrap per model load/rotate) and generally tiny, but if you do per-request HSM operations it can add up. we usually recommend customer-managed KMS with local HSM when high throughput and low-latency are required. action: ravi we'll capture typical KMS call counts in the next security deep-dive.
[03:28] Daniel: ok. back to batching — can you run with fixed batch sizes vs dynamic batching? we worry about tail latency spiking if batch windows are long.
[03:36] Ethan: absolutely. we can run two profiles: fixed small batch (8) and medium batch (32) with a per-batch max latency SLO and dynamic adaptive mode. initial numbers show medium batch (32) yields about 1.9x tokens/sec vs batch 8 but median latency improves, tail (95th) gets worse by ~170 ms in our tests. for interactive product like yours median is ok but for select flows you might need lower tail.
[04:06] Priya: that tail matters for our live chat handler. if latency goes high, re-renders happen and UX breaks. we prefer slightly lower throughput for better tail.
[04:16] Ethan: noted — we'll include 95/99 percentiles in the benchmark spreadsheet.
[04:21] Lina (CSM): quick note on cost model assumptions — maya can you confirm the unit costs included? we had earlier confusion between hosted list price vs pilot discounted hourly.
[04:30] Maya: yes, checked — sheet attached in the drive is pilot-discount numbers. i'll update one tab with list price and one with pilot price to make comparisons clear.
[04:38] Sonia: regarding model variants: are there lighter-weight models that give similar P95 quality but much better tokens/sec? we want quality to stay within 3% of current baseline.
[04:47] Ethan: there are a couple: Efficient-13B distilled and a 7B with extended context. the 7B with quant + optimized kernels gives about 2.6x tokens/sec vs the 13B but shows a 4–6% dip on some regen metrics. distillation of 13B gets closer — maybe 1.4x tokens/sec with <3% quality delta. we can run A/B on your prompts.
[05:12] Priya: ok please run A/B. we'll hand over 20 representative prompts that cover short, medium, and long context cases.
[05:19] Ethan: perfect — please attach them to the drive link.
[05:23] [05:23] (audio blip)
[05:26] Maya: quick question on measurement: when you say tokens/sec per dollar, are you using request-level tokens or total tokens including prefixes?
[05:33] Daniel: yeah that's important — prefixes change the denominator a lot.
[05:36] Ethan: our definition here is total compute tokens consumed per dollar of infra plus provisioning overhead for the pool. but for customer-facing KPIs you might want to use only generation tokens per request. i'll include both metrics in the sheet.
[05:47] Priya: great. also can caching introduce correctness issues? like stale prefix responses? we have compliance concerns.
[05:55] Ethan: caching is purely on the prefix/kv level for speed; it doesn't change generation for new tokens but it can return reused KV states. we do have TTLs and invalidation hooks. for PII-sensitive flows we'd recommend stricter TTLs and audit logs. we can also scope caching to non-PII routes.
[06:12] Ravi: what about encryption at rest for the cache store — is that customer-manageable?
[06:17] Maya: yes, cache storage at rest is encrypted; on private deployments you can plug in your own KMS/HSM and control keys. we'll surface the architecture doc in the security deep-dive.
[06:27] Sonia: timeline check — if we run the extended 5k-token benchmark, how long to get results?
[06:33] Ethan: depending on runs and variants maybe 3 business days — we allocate a small burst pool and run systematic tests. if we run 4 variants (13B baseline, 13B quant, 7B quant, 13B distilled) with cache on/off and 3 batch configs — it's ~2–3 days to get stable numbers.
[06:53] Priya: okay. can you also capture cost per completed request for our medium and long templates? that will help product decisioning.
[06:59] Ethan: yes — that'll be in the output sheet: cost/request, tokens/request, tokens/sec/$, median/95/99 latencies.
[07:07] Maya: any blockers on your side?
[07:10] Priya: none besides getting the 20 prompt templates uploaded. also want to verify if Redwood can redact sensitive fields before sending logs for observability.
[07:19] Lina: for pilot visibility we have a scrubber option in the console — it's a config to mask PII before logs leave the instance. we'll include that doc.
[07:28] Daniel: one more on competitors — you mentioned Anthropic earlier; is there a direct perf comparison we can see?
[07:35] Ethan: we have a rough public benchmark but it won't be apples-to-apples. we can do a targeted comparison using your prompts if helpful — would need permission to run traffic and some credits.
[07:47] Priya: let's hold that until after your internal run.
[07:51] Maya: ok closing the loop — recap: ethan will run the 5k token runs with cache on/off and three batch configs; priya will upload the 20 prompts; maya will update the cost model and strip pilot vs list pricing; raji — ravi will gather KMS/egress numbers for the security session. we'll plan security deep-dive week of Aug 24.
[08:09] Sonia: sounds good. thanks everyone.
[08:12] Maya: thanks all, we'll follow up with the sheet and a meeting invite for the security deep-dive. bye.
